title: Shortening the Diagnostic Odyssey for Children with Rare Pulmonary Diseases (RPD)
text:
This project aims to use artificial intelligence and genomic sequencing to shorten the diagnostic odyssey for
children with rare lung diseases and uncover new genetic insights. By quickly identifying children with hidden
genetic conditions and characterizing novel genetic contributions to rare pulmonary diseases, the research could
lead to earlier treatments, improving their health and reducing long-term complications. In the future, this AI-
driven approach may also help diagnose other serious conditions, enhancing health and reducing illness.

title: Dual p300 and p53 reactivation in HPV+ head and neck cancer
text:
Current treatments to manage HPV+ OPC patients are effective but not without limitations and, therefore, there
remains an urgent need to develop more active and less toxic drugs to optimally manage these patients in the
first-line and recurrent/metastatic settings. Our multi-disciplinary team developed a novel, dual p53 and p300
modulator to reactivate tumor suppressive programs in HPV+ OPC. This proposal will provide new insights on
the biological consequences of restoring p53 and p300 functionality, and results generated will be leveraged to
guide the drug development path of OHM1.

title: Core B: Technology, Assessment, Data, and Analysis Core
text: TADA Core The Technology, Assessment, Data, and Analysis (TADA) Core will support the Stress, Trauma, and Resil- ience (STAR) COBRE by leveraging novel technological, methodological, design and analytical approaches to support and enrich STAR research projects. Specifically, the TADA Core will provide support for an array of innovative, state-of-the-field methods—uniquely offering expertise in leveraging technology for observa- tional, laboratory and interventional studies critical for (1) obtaining ecologically valid data on stress exposures, and psychological, behavioral, and physiological responses with high temporal resolution, (2) novel ap- proaches to digital phenotyping, and (3) electronically-delivered adaptive interventions. During Phase 1, TADA was highly productive, supporting 106 researchers and providing nearly two dozen innovative workshops and trainings in laboratory, ecological, and wearable technologies. The TADA Core provided support for assess- ments including mixed quantitative and qualitative methods, data management, electronic data capture, and sophisticated statistical analysis for longitudinal, complex data. The core also established the STAR eye- tracking laboratory, the STAR ecological assessment hub, a qualitative and mixed methods hub, and a STAR biostatistics hub, including purchase of state-of-the-field equipment (e.g., Tobii eyetracker, centrifuge, biospeci- men freezers) and software (e.g.,Ilumivu EMA software, Mplus, Mindfield, eSense Plus, ArcGIS). The core also established a STAR measures repository. Building on the success of Phase 1, in Phase 2, the TADA core will refine and expand services and build a framework for long term sustainability. Our core will provide a sustainable resource to help investigators apply innovative, integrated methodological approaches, with ana- lytic approaches matched to the study of stress, trauma, and resilience and development of novel and scalable interventions. The core will scaffold STAR investigators, providing expertise and skill development using gold- standard and novel methodological approaches. Technological innovations progress rapidly, and TADA Core will provide a centralized resource for training and exchange of expertise relevant to innovative and emerg- ing technologies. In Phase 2 the TADA Core will build on the support of unique equipment and software (e.g., Biopac, LEAP actigraphs), expanding over time to meet the needs of the growing STAR research com- munity, and to expand to serve the larger community of Rhode Island investigators. In addition to an expanded focus on intervention development, the specific Aims of the TADA Core in Phase 2 are to: (1) Provide exper- tise and services to support study design, technology implementation, assessment, and statistical analyses for COBRE-affiliated projects; (2) Serve as a centralized resource for research training and exchange of methods, technology design, implementation, and analytic ideas related to the study of stress, trauma, and resilience; (3) Provide expertise and services to support data management and create a repository of data that can serve as a resource for STAR investigators, and (4) Explicitly build a framework for sustainability.

title: Immunoreceptors and Immunotherapy
text:
This application requests support for the FASEB conference on Immunoreceptors and
Immunotherapy that has been held biennially since 1987. This meeting will highlight the latest
technological advances in immune cell research, with a focus on understanding immune receptor
function and complexities of immunotherapy as well as bringing together leading experts and
early career investigators in the field. This conference is very important to human health because
it will help to drive discussion of new therapeutic strategies for harnessing the power of immune
cells and their receptors in targeting autoimmunity, infectious disease and cancer.

title: Th17 extracellular trap-mediated antimicrobial host defense in acne vulgaris
text:
RELEVANCE TO PUBLIC HEALTH
Acne, the most common human skin disease, is associated with C. acnes, affects over 50 million people in the
U.S., and has a significant psychological impact on patients affecting their self-esteem. This study will provide
greater fundamental insights into mechanisms of how T helper cells primed by healthy skin commensals serve
as a line of defense against breaching pathogens in acne. The discovery of C. acnes ligands will lead to the

title: CRISPR Based Rescue of Glaucoma in Lowe Syndrome
text:
Lowe syndrome is a rare disease in boys that causes glaucoma and cataracts, kidney failure, intellectual
disabilities, and seizures; there is no therapy for this severe vision- and life-threatening disease. In this proposal,
we are developing several groundbreaking strategies using CRISPR-mediated gene therapy to rescue OCRL
loss and serve as treatments for Lowe syndrome. The potential benefits of this proposed research include
development of the first effective treatment for a rare but severe pediatric disease: a chance to save vision and
prolong lives.

title: Regulation of Dopamine Transporter by Trafficking
text:
The neurotransmitter dopamine is essential for central nervous system control of locomotor activity, cognition
and reward mechanisms. As such, dopamine is involved in several neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric
disorders, such as Parkinson’s disease, schizophrenia, ADHD and drug addiction. Dopamine transporter (DAT)
serves to terminate dopamine neurotransmission and is a principal target of cocaine, methylphenidate and
amphetamines. Revealing the components and processes that regulate DAT in intact brain as proposed in this
application may lead to new strategies in the therapeutic intervention with drug addiction.

title: Cancer Genetics and Genomics Program
text: CANCER GENETICS AND GENOMICS PRORGRAM – PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT The Cancer Genetics and Genomics Program (CGG) at the Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cancer Center (CSHL-CC) develops and applies advanced genomic technologies to investigate the genetic and molecular basis of tumor biology, with a focus on cancer-associated immune and endocrine processes. The Program's research is organized around three principal aims: 1) the development of genomic methodologies for tracking clonal evolution, enhancing detection, and identifying therapeutic targets; 2) the application of genetic and computational tools to characterize tumor-immune interactions; and 3) the integration of genomic approaches to delineate hormonal regulation in cancer initiation, progression, and treatment response. The Program is co-led by Drs. Tobias Janowitz and Camila dos Santos and comprises 19 members with expertise in genomics, immunology, endocrinology, and computational biology. Over the past five years, CGG investigators have developed a suite of advanced genomic technologies, including long-read sequencing, CRISPR-based lineage tracing, novel murine models of cancer, and computational frameworks for evolutionary modeling. Through these tools and mechanistic studies, members have constructed high-resolution models of tumor–immune interactions, identified molecular mechanisms linking hormonal states during pregnancy or cachexia to neoplasia, and identified novel drivers of cancer development and progression. The Program emphasizes integration across experimental and computational domains, thus supporting the Center's strategic priorities in promoting cross- disciplinary collaborative research. Collaborations with clinical partners, particularly at Northwell Health, have enabled the translational application of genomic tools to mechanistic discovery research, biomarker development and early-phase trials. In the current period, CGG members have published 147 publications. Of these, 33 (22%) reflect intra-Programmatic collaborations, 35 (24%) inter-Programmatic collaborations, 127 (86%) collaborations with external institutions, and 89 (61%) collaborations with other NCI-designated cancer centers. In addition, 79 (54%) were published in journals with an impact factor exceeding 10. The Program holds 15 R01-equivalent cancer-focused awards across 9 members, with total peer-reviewed cancer-relevant funding increasing from $3.0M in 2020 to $4.8M in 2025, including $3.5M from the NCI. CGG research catalyzes discovery and innovation through integrative and collaborative cancer science. Its strategic focus on genetics, genomics, endocrinology, and computational biology is in turn aligned with the CSHL-CC research priorities and strategic plan, all while fostering career advancement across Program members and their trainees.

title: Microscopy Core
text: Project/Summary Abstract (Microscopy Core) The overall goal of the Microscopy Core is to provide Indiana Diabetes Research Center (IDRC) investigators with effective access to advanced methods of light microscopy that have been optimized for metabolic tissues. These powerful techniques include intravital microscopy and CODEX (CO-Detection by indEXing) imaging, developed during the previous grant period, and newly established techniques within the Core, including FLIM (Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging), expansion microscopy, and lightsheet microscopy. The Microscopy Core utilizes the extensive facilities of the Indiana Center for Biological Microscopy (ICBM), the Indiana University School of Medicine’s well-established core microscopy facility. The Core is equipped with three point-scanning confocal/multiphoton excitation microscopes and two Phenocycler-Fusion multiplex fluorescent imaging systems, as well as a spinning-disk confocal microscope and multiple digital workstations supporting quantitative two- and three-dimensional image analysis. The Core is fully equipped to support intravital microscopy, providing investigators with space in a surgical suite containing all necessary supplies for surgery, anesthesia, and animal monitoring. The Microscopy Core benefits not only from the extensive facilities of the ICBM, but also from the reliable performance of systems maintained by ICBM staff and continuously supported with manufacturers’ service contracts. Specifically, the Core will apply and adapt methods of intravital microscopy and CODEX developed internally and within the ICBM and the IDRC. Beyond the equipment and resources already in place, the ICBM recently purchased an Alpenglow Biosciences lightsheet microscope, which will be used in the next phase of development for new planned offerings in the Microscopy Core. The Microscopy Core is Directed by Dr. A. Linnemann. The Core leverages the expertise of a staff scientist and technician and interfaces closely with the Islet & Physiology Core of the IDRC to ensure that tissue resources and surgical expertise are tightly integrated. The Microscopy Core will achieve the following aims: (1) To provide IDRC investigators with assistance in the methods of quantitative intravital microscopy and the related implementation of fluorescent protein biosensors for intravital and in vitro studies. (2) To provide design and implementation assistance with CODEX imaging of pancreas and other tissues of interest to IDRC investigators. (3) To provide training in the methods of intravital microscopy and image analysis developed by the Core. (4) To provide technical support for laboratories lacking microscopy expertise to utilize additional challenging techniques. (5) To develop and expand Core offerings to include novel cutting edge imaging approaches such as FLIM, expansion microscopy, and lightsheet microscopy.

title: Investigating structural and biochemical factors guiding concanamycin A biosynthesis
text:
Concanamycin A (CMA) is a polyketide natural product produced by several bacterial species with major potential
therapeutic applications. The proposed work will focus on elucidating the structure of the cellular machinery that
synthesizes CMA and uncovering the mechanisms behind intracellular CMA storage. Insights from this work will
inform strategies for engineering CMA biosynthetic pathways and enhancing the production of CMA and its
analogs for therapeutic applications.

title: Estradiol regulation of an amygdala microcircuit for valence processing
text: Women are twice as likely as men to experience posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and estradiol signaling is implicated as a primary mechanism driving female susceptibility. In this proposal, we test the novel hypothesis that estradiol regulation of an amygdala circuit controlling negative valence leads to the development of persistent negative bias when intense acute stress is experienced under low estradiol states. Elucidation of this circuit may lead to new treatments for PTSD in women.

title: Semi-structured Information Retrieval in Clinical Text for Cohort Identification
text:
The widespread adoption of Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has enabled secondary use of EHR data for
clinical and translational research. We propose to advance informatics solutions to enable cohort discovery
using information retrieval and deep representation techniques.

title: Population Genomic Screening in Primary Care
text: Despite advances in our understanding of genomic basis of disease risk and advances in technology enabling genomic risk assessment, implementation of genomic medicine is limited. Many individuals at risk for common, actionable genomic conditions remain undiagnosed and most are unaware of their risk. Population. To generate evidence on feasibility and clinical utility, working with our community stakeholders, we will develop and implement a pilot program for population genomic screening for common, actionable genetic conditions in primary care.

title: Prefrontal-cingulate functional networks in aging monkeys: neural circuit substrates of cognitive aging
text:
Two key frontal cortical areas implicated in cognitive aging —the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) and anterior
cingulate cortex (ACC) -- participate in diverse in vivo functional “resting state” networks, but the neural basis of
in vivo MRI measures of connectivity and how they change with age has not been elucidated. Using multi-tiered
in vivo and ex vivo methods, the proposed study will assess age-related changes in functional MRI resting state
network dynamics and how these relate to cognitive decline, and cellular-molecular circuit properties in LPFC
and ACC. Understanding these macro- to micro-scale relationships is essential to developing novel in vivo MRI
biomarkers for neural circuit imbalances associated with cognitive impairments in aging, which can be extended
to related neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases.

title: mRNA stability and its impact on hematopoiesis and acute leukemia
text:
This application focuses on a family of RNA-binding proteins (ZFP36/TIS11) identified in our
screens are able to control “stemness” and differentiation of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells.
It tests the hypothesis that 3’UTR targeting of key hematopoiesis-regulating mRNAs by the
ZFP36/TIS11 family represents a novel posttranscriptional mechanism of stem cell differentiation
and leukemic transformation.

title: Experimental platforms for high-throughput characterization of asthma genes and pathways
text: PROJECT 2 — PROJECT SUMMARY The genetic architecture of asthma, like that of many other common diseases, is highly polygenic and influenced by a large number of genetic variants, most of them non-coding, each imparting small phenotypic effects on asthma risk. Motivating these large genetic mapping efforts is the notion that these genetic variants associated with asthma may provide key insights into asthma pathogenesis, but only if they are first connected to effector genes (variant to genes), and then that these genes are shown to impact pathways, cellular and/or molecular phenotypes (variant to function). Over the past 4 years, we focused on bridging the variant to gene aspect of this outstanding challenge. We successfully completed our goals, generating comprehensive regulatory maps in asthma-relevant cell types and developing novel statistical frameworks for fine-mapping loci associated with asthma. The deployment of these computational and experimental strategies resulted in the nomination of over 200 genes that may be causal to asthma pathogenesis. These genes often have pleiotropic effects across cell types, and the major cell types that appear enriched for asthma heritability are airway epithelial cells and T cells. The major goal of Project 2 of our AADCRC is to develop strategies to link candidate asthma causal genes with cellular and molecular functions in asthma-relevant cell types. Motivated by our discoveries in the first phase of our AADCRC, we developed platforms to assess cellular phenotypes commonly associated with asthma in bronchial epithelial cells and T cells. We successfully scaled these phenotypic platforms such that we can capitalize on CRISPR-based strategies and perturb hundreds of genes in human bronchial epithelial and T cells, measuring the phenotypic effects, if any, of these genetic perturbations. These scaled CRISPR screens of asthma candidate genes will receive as input 1) the approximately 200 candidate genes that we nominated in Phase 1 of our AADCRC,2) novel genes that will be nominated by the various strategies proposed in Project 1, and 3) novel genes nominated by a unique and rich multiomic dataset generated in primary human lung resident T cells, proposed in Aim 1 of this project. The cellular and molecular data generated in this project will be used by the Computational Genetics Core (CGC) to identify novel pathways that may be shared by genes involved in asthma pathogenesis. The development and use of the computational and experimental strategies proposed here will result in a fuller understanding of the genes and molecular/cellular mechanisms underlying the genetics of susceptibility to asthma.

title: Probing inflammation dynamics via multi-modal tracking and control of engineered macrophages
text:
This project aims to investigate inflammation dynamics through the development of engineered macrophages
capable of both tracking and modulating inflammatory responses in vivo. By integrating multimodal imaging
techniques, including ultrasound, MRI, and optical imaging, we will achieve a comprehensive understanding of
macrophage behavior at various spatial and temporal scales. Ultimately, this theranostic approach envisions
using living cells as therapeutic agents and imaging probes, paving the way for precision treatments of
inflammation-related diseases.

title: Project 2: Prenatal Alcohol Exposure (PAE) and Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD)
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health as an understanding of those molecular pathways that 
modify sensitivity to prenatal alcohol exposure-induced birth defects is expected in the long-term to inform 
clinical practice and ultimately reduce the incidence and severity of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD). 
This objective will be met by applying two innovative and complementary approaches to assess in cell and 
animal models if novel genes or chemicals modulate the deficits elicited by ethanol exposure. Thus, the 
proposed research is relevant to the parts of NIH/NIAAA’s mission that pertains to characterizing biological 
mechanisms underlying FASD, identifying biomarkers of prenatal alcohol exposure, and ultimately will reveal 
fundamental and novel insights into the mechanism of ethanol-induced birth defects.

title: Mapping the genomic and molecular mechanisms of antifungal resistance in the emerging fungal pathogen Candida auris
text:
Candida auris has rapidly emerged as a multi-drug resistant pathogen and public health threat associated
with significant morbidity and mortality. In 2019, a CDC report listed C. auris among the most urgent
antimicrobial resistance threats in the United States. It is of vital importance to understand how resistance
develops in C. auris, so that this knowledge can be translated into therapies that prolongs the lives of
affected individuals.

title: Investigating the effects of TCF4 mutations during oligodendrocyte development and maturation in a human-derived model of autism spectrum disorder
text:
This proposal aims to assess the effects of mutations in the critical brain developmental transcription
factor TCF4 during human oligodendrocyte development and maturation. As oligodendrocytes are
one of the few cell types in the brain that maintain a self-renewing, proliferative progenitor pool, this
work has the potential to shed light on the genetic regulation of oligodendrogenesis and serve as a
platform for screening and testing of pro-myelinating drugs and therapies. The long-term goal is to
identify a viable therapeutic approach to treat Pitt-Hopkins syndrome, a disease caused by mutations
in TCF4, and improve the patients' and families’ quality of life.
